findings.matters: A waste contract ending and being retendered or delivered in-house is a large recurring cost decision, and other councils facing similar retender decisions would compare the options and timing.

findings.matters: A decision on a leisure management contract, whether to extend or retender, carries a long-term cost and liability that finance officers and lenders would want to see once options are set out.

findings.matters: A capital grant programme whose completion was reported early and then slipped is the kind of delivery change a finance director would track against grant conditions and end dates.

findings.matters: Council tax income from second homes depends on the premium and on the stock of second homes, so a finance officer at another council would want to see whether a similar trend is happening locally.
findings.figures: Second homes 905 to 807 properties (down 98); holiday lets down 10 in the quarter

findings.detail: The paper gives Q1 outturn of 33.50% against a 33% Q1 target and Q2 outturn of 61.30% against a 61% Q2 target, with both quarters marked On track.
findings.matters: Council tax collection is a core income line, and a finance director would compare the in-year profile with peers' collection performance.
findings.figures: Q1 outturn 33.50% (Q1 target 33%); Q2 outturn 61.30% (Q2 target 61%); year-end target 98.4%

findings.detail: The paper reports Q1 outturn of 30.10% against a 28% Q1 target and Q2 outturn of 58.60% against a 61% Q2 target. It attributes the shortfall to payment timing, noting that one large business paying late can affect the figure.
findings.matters: Business rates income depends on a small number of large payers, so a finance director elsewhere would want to see how a single payment can move the in-year collection figure.
findings.figures: Q1 outturn 30.10% (Q1 target 28%); Q2 outturn 58.60% (Q2 target 61%); Q4 target 97.3%
findings.quote: It only takes one large business to delay making payment for the performance to be adversely impacted.

findings.matters: A finance director at another council would want to know when a district's gap-closing plan reaches members and how it is framed, and a lender would want the size of the gap once it is reported.

findings.matters: Prompt supplier payment is a standard finance performance measure and affects supplier relations and any late-payment exposure.
findings.quote: The number of undisputed invoices paid on time was again above 99%

findings.detail: The report records sickness absence above target in Q2 2026/27. It is one of the KPIs marked as not achieved.

findings.matters: Business rates collection rates feed directly into a council's cash flow and its share of retained rates, so a shortfall in collection is relevant to finance officers here and at peer councils.

Social Housing Grant Tideswell (£450,000) and Disabled Facilities Grants (£210,277) also move into 2027/28. findings.headline: The council says borrowing for future capital schemes is unlikely to be affordable for the revenue account.

findings.matters: A council stating that borrowing is not affordable for future capital schemes is relevant to lenders and to peers weighing the same choice.

findings.detail: The paper says the figure excludes grants, section 106 contributions and strategic reserves, which are held for specific purposes. It describes the risk to future funding as high and says borrowing is unlikely to be affordable for the revenue account.
findings.matters: It shows how little uncommitted own-resource capital funding remains for future schemes, and that the council is ruling out borrowing as the fallback.

findings.detail: The paper says the reserves fund the programme but would be drawn down substantially over five years. The table in Appendix 3 shows the total at £5,947,287 at 1 April 2028 and £6,051,408 at 31 March 2031.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at a peer council, can see how much capital funding remains once a five-year programme is committed, and how quickly it is used.

findings.quote: sources of capital funding are forecast to reduce from £15.8m at 1st April 2026 to £6.0m by 31st March 2031

findings.detail: The report links the staffing overspend to a higher turnover provision and a pay award above budget. Services are using temporary agency staff to meet statutory responsibilities, and the turnover provision will be reviewed in the 2027/28 budget.
findings.matters: The turnover provision is a common budgeting device that councils may need to revisit when vacancies fall, and the agency cost of filling gaps is visible here.

findings.headline: Kennelling costs exceed budget in an ongoing legal matter, with a report to Members to follow.
findings.detail: The council reports a £53k forecast pressure on kennelling budgets. The report describes this as an ongoing legal matter and says a separate report will go to Members.
findings.matters: A legal matter driving an unbudgeted service cost is a pressure other councils may face and a potential contingent liability.
findings.figures: £53k forecast pressure on kennelling budget
findings.quote: In response to an ongoing situation, the Council is incurring kennelling costs that exceed the current budget. This is an ongoing legal matter, a report will be presented to Members in due course.

findings.headline: Council has identified a 'Financial Resilience' risk on its Strategic Risk Register, rated high, pending savings delivery and the 2027/28 settlement.
findings.detail: The risk report states that Financial Resilience is assessed as high risk and lists consequences of not identifying the required savings. The report says the budget principles will help to mitigate the risk, but the council also rates the financial risk of the report's recommendations as low.
findings.matters: A council that rates its own financial resilience as high risk while pursuing reserve-based gap closure is a position that lenders and auditors will track.
findings.quote: “Financial Resilience” has been identified on the Council’s Strategic Risk Register and has been assessed as high risk, pending the delivery of the required savings

findings.headline: Reserves forecast to fall from £27,341,145 at 31 March 2026 to £12,203,013 at 31 March 2028, with the Revenue General Reserve forecast at £2,483,095 in 2027/28.
findings.detail: Appendix 3 shows total reserves falling in 2026/27 through transfers, including capital programme spending and a £2.3m draw on capital receipts. Earmarked reserves fall from £18,568,079 to £7,378,751 by 2027/28, with the S106 reserve and Vehicle Renewals reserve among the largest reductions.
findings.matters: A large planned run-down of earmarked and capital reserves within two years is directly relevant to the sustainability of reserve-funded budgets elsewhere.
findings.figures: £27,341,145 total reserves at 31 March 2026; £15,940,394 forecast at 31 March 2027; £12,203,013 forecast at 31 March 2028; £18,568,079 earmarked reserves at 31 March 2026; £7,378,751 earmarked reserves forecast at 31 March 2028

findings.headline: Council proposes to transfer the 2026/27 underspend to the Funding Uncertainties Reserve and defer any decision on its use until LGR is clearer.
findings.detail: The report recommends that no decision is made on the forecast underspend at this stage. The uncertainty around leisure and waste contract renewals from 2028/29 is cited as the reason to hold the underspend in reserve. The LGR Reserve stands at £421,871 and any use requires Council approval.
findings.matters: A decision to hold year-end surpluses in an uncertainties reserve, rather than applying them to the gap, is a choice other councils facing similar contract renewals will want to compare.
findings.figures: £510,762 underspend proposed for transfer; £421,871 LGR Reserve balance
findings.quote: it is recommended that any underspend at out-turn for 2026/27 be transferred to the Funding Uncertainties Reserve.

findings.headline: Medium-Term Financial Plan shows savings required of £716,600 in 2027/28 rising to £3,452,000 in 2029/30, after a one-year delay to Local Government Reorganisation.
findings.detail: The Secretary of State has announced LGR in Derbyshire from 1 April 2029, a one-year delay, so the council must now address both the 2027/28 and 2028/29 gaps. The MTFP shows the required savings, additional income or reserve use of £2.4m for 2028/29 and £0.7m for 2027/28. The Corporate Leadership Team has identified potential savings of £2.9m, which are subject to member review.
findings.matters: A council with multi-year gaps that rise through the plan period, with the timing of the gap moved by LGR, is a useful comparator for other councils setting their own medium-term savings targets.
findings.quote: The MTFP indicates that savings will be required from 2027/28 in order to set a balanced budget.

findings.headline: Planning fee income forecast £300k above budget, with the report describing it as a one-off driven by a single major application worth £258k in fees.
findings.detail: Planning income is forecast to exceed budget by £300k. The report says this is largely attributable to one major application generating £258k of fees, and treats the overachievement as one-off rather than recurring.
findings.matters: Reliance on a single large application to close a budget gap is a concentration risk that finance officers elsewhere would want to recognise when assessing one-off versus recurring income.
findings.figures: £300k forecast overachievement; £258k fees from a single major application
findings.quote: the £300k forecast overachievement is considered a one-off benefit. This is largely attributable to a single major application, which generated planning fees of £258k.

findings.headline: Investment income forecast at £281k above revised budget, with the council assuming a 4% average return against a base rate held at 3.75% rather than the 3.5% assumed in the budget.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 investment income budget was £529k at Quarter 1. By 30 September £491k had been received and a further £319k is anticipated. The budget had assumed the Bank of England base rate would fall to 3.5% by 1 April 2026, but it has held at 3.75% for the first two quarters.
findings.matters: Treasury and cash-balance income is a rate-sensitive source of surplus that peers and lenders will want to see tested against the rate path.
findings.figures: £529k revised budget at Quarter 1; £491k received; £319k further anticipated; £281k forecast surplus; 4% assumed average rate; 3.75% base rate; 3.5% budgeted rate

findings.detail: The forecast underspend has grown from £376,418 at Quarter 1. The report recommends that any year-end underspend go to the Funding Uncertainties Reserve rather than being spent.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the size and drivers of a mid-year underspend, and the split between one-off and recurring items, against their own position.
findings.figures: £510,762 forecast underspend; £376,418 Quarter 1 forecast underspend; £16,475,532 proposed revised budget
findings.quote: The forecast out-turn position at quarter 2 for the Council is an underspend of £510,762.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Draft Community Asset Transfer Policy
findings.headline: Derbyshire Dales's policy sets an indicative six-month timeline for a simple transfer and a scoring framework weighting community benefit at 30% and financial sustainability at 20%
findings.detail: Appendix A notes that a simple and straightforward transfer is likely to take approximately six months. Appendix E sets out assessment weightings for applications, with community benefit at 30%, financial sustainability at 20%, governance and capacity at 20%, strategic fit at 15%, environmental benefit at 10%, and deliverability and risk at 5%.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing CAT processes across councils would see how much weight the council gives to financial sustainability versus community benefit, and the expected time to complete a transfer.
findings.figures: approximately six months; community benefit 30%; financial sustainability 20%; governance & capacity 20%; strategic fit 15%; environmental benefit 10%; deliverability & risk 5%
findings.quote: As a guide, a simple and straightforward transfer is likely to take approximately six months

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Draft Community Asset Transfer Policy
findings.headline: Derbyshire Dales's policy allows the council to reject a CAT application where retaining the asset is judged necessary for financial considerations
findings.detail: The council reserves the right not to progress or approve a CAT where retention is necessary to support its strategic priorities, service delivery, regeneration, financial considerations or asset management objectives, and the policy states that no entitlement to transfer is created by submitting an expression of interest or full application.
findings.matters: Finance officers at other councils would note that the discretion to refuse on financial grounds is open-ended, which affects how far applicants and lenders can rely on a transfer proceeding.
findings.quote: The Council reserves the right not to progress or approve a Community Asset Transfer application where it considers that retention of the asset is necessary to support the Council's strategic priorities, service delivery requirements, regeneration objectives, financial considerations

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Draft Community Asset Transfer Policy
findings.headline: Derbyshire Dales lists assets it will not consider for transfer, including all pay-and-display car parks, named major parks, depots and the Matlock Town Hall
findings.detail: The policy sets out a table of asset types excluded from CAT consideration, covering pay-and-display car parks, major parks, named land and buildings such as Matlock Town Hall and depots, cemeteries, war memorials, trust land and investment properties.
findings.matters: A finance director would see which parts of the council's estate are being kept out of transfer, which matters for planning of disposals and for income-generating assets such as car parks and investment property.
findings.quote: All Pay and display car parks and areas under parking orders

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Draft Community Asset Transfer Policy
findings.headline: Derbyshire Dales states that CAT assets are transferred at nil cost to the council, with the applicant normally paying legal, valuation and survey fees
findings.detail: Assets available for transfer are to be transferred in their current condition, at nil cost to the Council and at its discretion, with the applicant normally responsible for all legal, valuation, survey and other professional fees incurred by both parties. The policy also says the CAT process is not designed to provide grant funding.
findings.matters: A finance officer at another council considering a similar scheme would see that the council seeks to pass transaction costs to applicants and to avoid providing grant or direct financial support through the transfer process.
findings.figures: nil cost to the Council
findings.quote: Assets that are available for transfer will be transferred in their current condition, at nil cost to the Council and at the discretion of the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Draft Community Asset Transfer Policy
findings.headline: Derbyshire Dales draft policy sets a presumption that community asset transfers are made by lease or management agreement rather than freehold, with a clawback that tapers over 25 years
findings.detail: The policy states a presumption in favour of a management agreement or lease, with freehold reserved for exceptional cases such as considerable investment by the recipient. For community organisations, transfers are by lease with restrictions on use, permission required for disposal, and a clawback on future sale that tapers over 25 years.
findings.matters: A finance director weighing disposals against retained asset value would want to know that the council intends to keep ownership and a claw-back on value, which affects capital receipts and the exposure to future liabilities on transferred assets.
findings.figures: 25 years (clawback taper period)
findings.quote: there is a presumption in favour of a management agreement or lease as this will give the option to the Council of continuing to provide services from the asset

findings.headline: Council is incurring kennelling costs exceeding budget (£53k overspend) linked to an 'ongoing legal matter' with no detail provided in the report.
findings.detail: The paper discloses a £53k overspend on kennelling but offers only that 'this is an ongoing legal matter' with 'a report will be presented to Members in due course'. No detail on the nature, duration, or estimated resolution cost of this matter is provided, creating transparency gap.
findings.matters: Unquantified legal liabilities are a concern for lenders; a legal matter sufficient to cause £53k quarterly overspend may represent a larger hidden exposure or signal governance/compliance issues.
findings.figures: Kennelling budget pressure: £53k (forecast annual overspend, implies £13.25k per quarter)
findings.quote: In response to an ongoing situation, the Council is incurring kennelling costs that exceed the current budget. This is an ongoing legal matter, a report will be presented to Members in due course.

findings.headline: Local government reorganisation uncertainty is explicitly flagged as having 'important implications' for financial strategy; the council will defer reserve-allocation decisions pending clarity on LGR costs and structure.
findings.detail: The council notes that LGR uncertainty has 'important implications for the Council's financial strategy and medium-term financial resilience' and specifically recommends deferring any decision on allocating the Q1 underspend 'pending the delivery of the required savings and the outcome of the Local Government Finance Settlement for 2027/28 and beyond' and 'anticipated one-off LGR transition costs'. This suggests LGR is a material financial risk factor.
findings.matters: A council facing reorganisation/merger is higher financial risk: it cannot commit to multi-year savings plans, will face one-off transition costs, and may lose economies of scale or absorb a weaker authority's debts.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: The uncertainty surrounding Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) has important implications for the Council's financial strategy and medium-term financial resilience.

findings.headline: Council faces organisational resilience issues and is allocating £50k from the forecast underspend to the recruitment and retention reserve to address them.
findings.detail: The paper allocates £50k of the Q1 underspend to recruitment and retention reserve 'to ensure that there is an adequate balance available...to fund the proposals to address organisational resilience issues'. These issues are the subject of a separate report to the same council meeting, indicating management has identified problems beyond routine staffing management.
findings.matters: Organisational resilience issues—typically HR, morale, retention, or capability problems—create operational risk and can impair service delivery or drive unforeseen cost increases.
findings.figures: Reserve allocation for resilience: £50k
findings.quote: £50,000 be transferred to the recruitment and retention reserve to ensure that there is an adequate balance available in the reserve to fund the proposals to address organisational resilience issues that are the subject of a report elsewhere on the agenda for this meeting.

findings.headline: Staffing costs overrunning by £119k due to turnover provision tripled from £95k to £336k and pay award higher than budgeted.
findings.detail: The turnover provision was increased 'in response to recurring staffing underspends arising from vacant posts and staff turnover, and to bring the budget more in line with those of other Derbyshire authorities'. Pay award came in at 3.3% against a 3% budget. This indicates persistent staff retention problems and rising employment costs that are recurring, not one-off.
findings.matters: Staffing is typically the largest cost item in local government; if retention costs are rising faster than income and require multiple years of catch-up provision, this signals structural cost pressure.
findings.figures: Staffing overspend 2026/27: £119k; Turnover provision increased from £95k to £336k; Pay award: 3.3% vs 3% budgeted
findings.quote: Staffing budgets are forecast to overspend by £119k. This is mainly due to an increased staff turnover provision included in the 2026/27 budget, which rose from £95k to £336k, and the impact of the 2026/27 pay award, which was 3.3% rather than the budgeted 3.0%.

findings.headline: Q1 underspend of £376k is driven by two one-off income items that will not recur: £281k investment income upside and £200k planning fees from a single major application.
findings.detail: The apparent underspend masks a weaker underlying position. Investment income outperformance (£281k) stems from interest rates holding at 3.75% rather than the budgeted assumption of 3.5% by April—this is contingent on rates and non-recurring. Planning income (£200k surplus) is explicitly labelled a one-off, 'largely attributable to a single major application, which generated planning fees of £258k'. Together these account for £481k of the £376k reported underspend.
findings.matters: A lender interpreting the Q1 underspend as evidence of good budget management would be misled; the underlying run-rate position is weaker because these income sources are not structural.
findings.figures: Q1 underspend: £376.418k; Investment income outperformance: £281k; Planning income one-off: £200k (from single application)
findings.quote: the £200k forecast overachievement is considered a one-off benefit. This is largely attributable to a single major application, which generated planning fees of £258k.

findings.headline: Council increased its budget by £1.75m (12%) in the first three months via virements from earmarked reserves.
findings.detail: After setting a net revenue budget of £14.278m in March 2026, the council approved £1.749m in supplementary budgets by end June 2026, funded entirely from reserves for projects 'where timing has been uncertain'. This mid-year budget expansion to £16.028m suggests either initial underestimation or project cost overruns and raises questions about budget accuracy.
findings.matters: A lender sees a 12% budget increase in the first quarter as a warning sign of either poor budget discipline or emerging cost pressures not anticipated when the annual budget was set.
findings.figures: Original budget 2026/27: £14,278,677; Revised budget after virements: £16,027,950; Virement total: £1,749,273
findings.quote: Since the budget was formally approved, there has been a number of virements approved under delegated authority which has impacted directorate totals. These additional approved budget changes are summarised in Appendix 1 and have the overall effect of increasing the budget by £1,749,273.

findings.headline: Council is using prior-year surpluses and drawing down reserves to bridge budget shortfalls; reserves forecast to fall from £27.3m to £12.3m by end 2028/29.
findings.detail: The council used a prior-year surplus of £1.287m to fund the 2026/27 budget and plans to use the 2026/27 forecast underspend (£250k) plus 2025/26 underspend (£424k forecast) to partially fund the 2027/28 gap. Starting reserves of £27.3m are forecast to decline to £14.6m by March 2027 and £12.3m by March 2028. This strategy works only if underspends continue and is not a sustainable funding model.
findings.matters: A lender is concerned when a council relies on reserve depletion to meet budget; reserves provide the buffer for emergencies, and their depletion signals structural problems are worsening, not being solved.

findings.quote: Use of prior year surplus to fund 2026/27 budget gap [£1,287k]; Use of 2025/26 underspend (as forecast at quarter 2) to partially fund 2027/28 budget gap [£424k]

findings.headline: Financial resilience is rated as high risk on the council's own strategic risk register, pending delivery of required savings.
findings.detail: The council's risk register identifies Financial Resilience as high risk, with potential consequences including lack of resources for core activities, controls being overlooked due to resource pressure, cash flow problems, and failure to perform capital maintenance programmes. This formal assessment underscores the severity of the structural position.
findings.matters: A lender is concerned when a council formally assesses its own financial resilience as high risk; this is the finance director's own warning signal.
findings.figures: Formal risk rating: high
findings.quote: 'Financial Resilience' has been identified on the Council's Strategic Risk Register and has been assessed as high risk, pending the delivery of the required savings and the outcome of the Local Government Finance Settlement for 2027/28 and beyond.

findings.headline: Structural funding deficit of £990.5k in 2027/28, escalating to £4.182m by 2029/30, requires savings the council has not yet identified.
findings.detail: The Medium Term Financial Plan shows the council will need to find savings of nearly £1m in 2027/28 just to balance the budget, with the gap widening sharply in subsequent years. The updated MTFP incorporates Q1 variances but contains no plan to close these gaps; the council's response is to defer reserve-allocation decisions pending LGR uncertainty.
findings.matters: A council unable to identify savings to close a structural deficit faces statutory breach of the duty to set a balanced budget; a lender needs to know whether this council can deliver the required reductions.
findings.quote: The MTFP indicates that savings will be required from 2027/28 in order to set a balanced budget.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Update Quarter 1 Sept Council 2026
findings.headline: Inflation on construction costs presents 'high financial risk' to capital programme despite contingencies
findings.detail: Section 7.1 explicitly notes that inflation and unforeseen events present 'a high financial risk to the overall capital programme.' While some larger projects include contingencies, the report states that 'even with these measures in place, the risk of overspend cannot be eliminated', with overall risk assessed as medium.
findings.matters: Combined with imminent reserve depletion, inflation-driven overruns could force further project cancellations or require external funding the council states it cannot afford.
findings.figures: Risk to programme assessed as: high (inflation), medium (overall)
findings.quote: While inflation on construction costs and additional costs arising from unforeseen events present a high financial risk to the overall capital programme, this report seeks to set accurate budgets for projects based upon previous tendering experience.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Update Quarter 1 Sept Council 2026
findings.headline: Council cancels £80k solar panel scheme for council housing between July and September 2026
findings.detail: Project 719 (Tansley Fern Close solar panels) was approved in July 2026 but cancelled by September 2026 before any expenditure. The scheme would have installed solar panels and upgraded eight council properties from EPC rating B to A. The council states available resources must be prioritised toward housing schemes with greater investment need.
findings.matters: Demonstrates that capital constraints are forcing cancellation of previously-approved schemes, and shows real pressure from reserve depletion on service delivery.
findings.quote: Whilst £80,000 was previously allocated to install solar panels and improve the properties to an EPC rating of A, the scheme will not be progressed at this time.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Update Quarter 1 Sept Council 2026
findings.headline: Council states future capital borrowing is unlikely to be affordable given medium-term financial position
findings.detail: The report notes that while borrowing for future capital schemes could be considered, the resulting borrowing costs 'are unlikely to be affordable for the revenue account, given the Council's medium term financial position.' This severely limits the council's options for funding capital investment beyond cash reserves.
findings.matters: Signals the council has constrained revenue budget and limited financing flexibility, which affects its capacity to fund service delivery and ability to service debt.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The Council could, of course, consider borrowing for future capital schemes, but the resulting borrowing costs are unlikely to be affordable for the revenue account, given the Council's medium term financial position.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Update Quarter 1 Sept Council 2026
findings.headline: Usable capital reserves forecast to fall from £15.1m to £5.9m over five years, leaving only £331k for new general fund schemes
findings.detail: The council's total available capital funding will reduce significantly by 2031. More critically, when restricted funding (grants, S106 contributions, strategic reserves) is excluded, only approximately £331k will remain in general capital receipts and capital programme reserves for new schemes. The report itself identifies this as presenting 'a high risk in terms of funding availability for future projects.'
findings.matters: Indicates severe constraint on the council's ability to fund new capital initiatives or respond to unexpected capital needs, which directly affects financial flexibility and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Opening balance 1 April 2026: £15.143m; forecast 31 March 2031: £5.926m; available for new schemes: circa £331k
findings.quote: sources of capital funding are forecast to reduce from £15.1m at 1st April 2026 to £5.9m by 31st March 2031

findings.headline: Ashbourne Reborn regeneration project carries high assessed risk despite being on track
findings.detail: A £15.2m capital regeneration scheme (Ashbourne Reborn, funded via Levelling Up) is being managed by the council as the Accountable Body. The council has assessed the risks as 'high' and is managing them through nominated officers and finance staff liaison to ensure grant claims are accurate and timely. The project is on track for completion in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A £15.2m capital scheme that is the council's responsibility as Accountable Body carries concentration risk. High assessed risk means the council has identified material things that could go wrong. If the project slips or faces cost overruns, it could impact the council's balance sheet and reserves.
findings.figures: £15.2m capital project; project completion scheduled for 2026/27
findings.quote: There are risks associated with the Accountable Body status for the Ashbourne Reborn Levelling Up scheme, which is a £15.2m capital project to regenerate Ashbourne town centre. These risks are significant and have been assessed as 'high'.

findings.headline: Monitoring Officer resigned during 2025/26; recruitment ongoing with interim arrangements in place
findings.detail: The council's Monitoring Officer—a statutory role responsible for ensuring lawfulness and ethical standards—resigned during the financial year. Interim arrangements have been put in place while recruitment proceeds. This is a key governance role with personal statutory duties.
findings.matters: The Monitoring Officer role is critical to ensuring the council operates within law and maintains governance standards. A vacant statutory post creates execution risk on compliance and ethics oversight. The longer the interim period, the greater the residual risk.
findings.figures: Monitoring Officer role vacant during 2025/26; recruitment ongoing
findings.quote: The Council's Monitoring Officer resigned during 2025/26, and interim arrangements were put in place while recruitment takes place.

findings.headline: Council tax and non-domestic rates collection fell slightly under target in 2025/26, attributed to cost of living crisis
findings.detail: The revenues and benefits service, delivered by Chesterfield Borough Council, achieved all KPIs in 2025/26 except for council tax collection (in-year and prior year) and non-domestic rates (in-year). These underperformed their targets. The statement attributes this to the cost of living crisis and notes that recovery action is continuing.
findings.matters: Collection rates directly affect the income available to fund services and close the budget gap. Falling rates in a cost-of-living crisis environment suggest the underlying trend may worsen before it improves, worsening the financial sustainability picture.
findings.figures: Council tax (in-year and prior year) collection and non-domestic rates (in-year) collection: slightly under target
findings.quote: In 2025/26 Chesterfield Borough Council achieved all the key performance indicators in the Revenues and Benefits contract, except for those relating to in-year and prior year collection of council tax and in-year collection of non-domestic rates, which were slightly under target. Payments have been impacted by the 'cost of living' crisis. Recovery action is continuing.

findings.headline: Significant budget gap in future years with no savings plan yet in place
findings.detail: The council has balanced the 2026/27 budget but faces a significant budget gap in future years identified in the Medium-Term Financial Plan. The statement explicitly identifies this as a significant governance issue and requires a savings plan to be developed by November 2026, with an updated MTFP and balanced budget for 2027/28 by March 2027. As of the statement date, this plan does not yet exist.
findings.matters: A council that cannot project a path to financial sustainability is a credit risk. The gap is material enough to be flagged as a governance issue, and the extended timeline to address it (not until March 2027) means there is no current plan for closing it.
findings.figures: Significant budget gap identified for future years; balanced budget set for 2026/27 only
findings.quote: The Council's Medium-Term Financial Plan identifies a significant budget gap in future years. To mitigate this risk, the Council has a Medium-Term Financial Strategy and Medium-Term Financial Plan in place. A balanced budget has been set for 2026/27, However, a savings plan must be developed to show how the Authority plans to address the budget gap for future years. This has been identified as a significant governance issue.

findings.paper_title: 1a Internal Audit Annual Report 2025.26 Appendix 1 v2
findings.headline: Assurance & Monitoring weaknesses account for 21 of 59 audit recommendations (36%), the dominant root cause category
findings.detail: Of 59 audit recommendations across 2025/26, 21 stem from Assurance & Monitoring failures—defined as unclear responsibility for checking, not identifying or acting on recurring problems, checking the wrong things, or under-sampling. This is the dominant root cause category by far, suggesting controls exist but are not being verified or overseen properly.
findings.matters: Controls that are not monitored are controls that may be silently failing. A 36% concentration in monitoring failures means the council has weak oversight of its financial and operational controls, increasing the risk of undetected errors or fraud.
findings.figures: Assurance & Monitoring: 21 recommendations out of 59 total (36%)
findings.quote: Root Cause Number of Recommendations % Assurance & Monitoring 21 36

findings.headline: Grants to Voluntary and Community Organisations received Limited Assurance on first audit, indicating weak controls over discretionary grants.
findings.detail: Grants to Voluntary and Community Organisations is a new audit receiving Limited Assurance, meaning controls over how grants are awarded, monitored and accounted for are either missing or ineffective. The council cannot be confident that grant spending achieves its intended objectives or complies with requirements.
findings.matters: Poor grant controls create exposure to misuse of public money, non-compliance with funding conditions, and potential clawback of external grants. Lenders and auditors scrutinise weak grant governance as a sign of broader control failure.
findings.figures: Grants to Voluntary and Community Organisations: Limited Assurance (new audit)

findings.paper_title: 1a Internal Audit Annual Report 2025.26 Appendix 1 v2
findings.headline: Housing Rents and Housing Contract Compliance received Limited Assurance on first audit, indicating new control weaknesses in the council's housing stock management.
findings.detail: Housing Rents and Housing Contract Compliance is a new audit area in 2025/26 and immediately received Limited Assurance, the lowest passing grade. Limited Assurance means certain important controls are either not in place or not operating effectively, creating risk that the system may not achieve its objectives. This is the council's first formal assessment of this area.
findings.matters: Housing income is a material revenue stream for councils, and control weaknesses in rent collection and contract compliance expose the council to revenue loss and financial mismanagement. This is a red flag for lenders on municipal housing viability.

findings.headline: Substantial assurance audits fell from 28% to 14% of the portfolio, a significant drop in control quality.
findings.detail: In 2024/25, five audits received Substantial Assurance (28% of 18 audits). In 2025/26, only two audits received Substantial Assurance (14% of 14 audits). Conversely, Reasonable Assurance audits increased from 61% to 72%. This shift indicates a broad weakening of control environments across the council's operations.
findings.matters: Declining assurance levels suggest the council's control framework is deteriorating, increasing risk to financial management and compliance. Lenders rely on strong internal controls to manage council finances.
findings.figures: Substantial Assurance: 5 (28%) in 2024/25 vs 2 (14%) in 2025/26. Reasonable Assurance: 11 (61%) in 2024/25 vs 10 (72%) in 2025/26.

findings.headline: Significant unforeseen repair costs signalling asset condition issues
findings.detail: Repairs and maintenance budget exceeded by £97k due to significant unforeseen work at multiple locations including Town Hall, Northwood Depot and Bakewell riverbank. The report acknowledges this is a reactive budget and flags that further review is needed to ensure adequate resource allocation.
findings.matters: Reactive maintenance pressures indicate aging assets in poor condition, which may require substantial capital investment ahead.
findings.figures: £97k repairs overspend
findings.quote: The repairs and maintenance budget is forecast to exceed budget by £97k as a result of significant unforeseen repair and maintenance work at numerous locations across the District, including the Town Hall, Northwood Depot and Bakewell riverbank. It is acknowledged that the repairs and maintenance budget is a reactive one and further review of this budget is to take place to ensure adequate budget resource is allocated.

findings.headline: Investment income overspend dependent on interest rates staying above budget assumptions
findings.detail: The council is forecasting £364k overachievement of investment income because base rates have remained higher than the 3.5% assumption made when the budget was set. However, the report notes this forecast 'is based on a number of assumptions and will continue to be refined throughout the financial year', and rates have already started falling (now 3.75% vs 3.5% budgeted).
findings.matters: A key driver of the reported underspend is rate-sensitive income that could reverse if base rates fall further, which would expose underlying structural deficits more quickly.
findings.figures: £364k investment income overachievement; base rate now 3.75% vs 3.5% budgeted
findings.quote: The base rate has subsequently reduced to 4% on 7th August and again to 3.75% on 17th December 2025, but as this is still over and above the budgeted base rate the Council continues to receive better returns on investments than anticipated.

findings.headline: Council explicitly warns of high-risk financial pressures from 2027/28 onwards
findings.detail: The Strategic Risk Register identifies Financial Resilience as high risk, pending delivery of required savings. The report states that significant financial challenges have been highlighted in the MTFP from 2027/28 onwards, and the council is creating a new Financial Sustainability Reserve to manage the transition. The report emphasises that creation of this reserve 'does not remove the underlying financial pressures' and that 'a comprehensive and sustainable savings programme will need to be developed and delivered'.
findings.matters: This is the council explicitly warning that structural deficits are forecast and that achieving balance will require major savings in the medium term, which is a core lender concern.
findings.figures: £1,221,081 forecast underspend being transferred to Financial Sustainability Reserve
findings.quote: Financial Resilience has been identified on the Council's Strategic Risk Register and has been assessed as high risk, pending the delivery of the required savings due to the outcome of the Local Government Finance Settlement for 2026/27 and beyond.

findings.headline: Council forecasting £258k additional income from waste default notices due to continuing route optimisation service deficiencies, budgeted as ongoing from 2026/27 onwards
findings.detail: The council is forecasting £258k additional income from waste default notices, described as resulting from 'continuing route optimisation service deficiencies'. The report explicitly flags this as an ongoing issue that has been built into the 2026/27 budget, indicating a persistent operational problem.
findings.matters: The council is relying on penalty income to offset service delivery failures, which is financially fragile and signals operational risk.
findings.figures: £258k additional income from waste default notices
findings.quote: an additional £258k income will be achieved through waste default notices because of continuing route optimisation service deficiencies. This is considered to be an ongoing issue, and provision has been made for additional income in the revenue budget for 2026/27 onwards.

findings.headline: Structural income losses locked into future budgets
findings.detail: Car parking income is down £35k permanently due to the 30 minutes free parking policy, and recycling credits are down £59k due to material market conditions. Both are described as ongoing reductions and have been built into the 2026/27 budget. This means future budgets start from a lower baseline.
findings.matters: These represent permanent revenue reductions that will constrain the council's financial flexibility going forward.
findings.figures: £35k car parking underspend, £59k recycling credits reduction
findings.quote: This pressure is anticipated to be a permanent reduction in car parking income and therefore has been included in the medium-term financial plan approved by Council on 5th March 2026.

findings.paper_title: 1. Supplementary budget to support microsme businesses and communities Council 5march2026
findings.headline: Council acknowledges forecast funding gaps and potential need for savings from 2027/28 onwards, the period when this grant commitment is active.
findings.detail: The report explicitly warns that the council has forecast funding gaps and may need to identify savings starting in 2027/28. The council notes it may also need to use reserves further to manage timing differences in savings delivery. These warnings apply while the council is committing to fund ongoing grant schemes with reserve drawdowns.
findings.matters: The council is signalling financial stress and uncertainty about its ability to maintain discretionary spending, raising questions about the durability of this two-year funding commitment.
findings.figures: Savings requirements potential 2027/28 onwards; no specific amounts quantified in this paper
findings.quote: The potential need to identify savings in 2027/28 onwards, alongside the potential further use of reserves to manage timing differences in savings delivery

findings.paper_title: 1. Supplementary budget to support microsme businesses and communities Council 5march2026
findings.headline: Council is drawing £300,000 from reserves for ongoing discretionary spending, rated medium risk due to forecast budget gaps.
findings.detail: The council proposes using reserves totalling £300,000 (£150,000 per year for 2026-27 and 2027-28) to continue grant schemes. The council explicitly rates this as medium risk, stating that ordinarily the risk would be low, but forecast funding gaps mean future savings requirements cannot be ruled out. The council may need to use reserves further to manage timing of savings delivery.
findings.matters: Using reserves for ongoing spending rather than capital investment or one-off costs, while expecting budget gaps, suggests financial stress and potential vulnerability of these programmes to future cuts.
findings.figures: £300,000 over two years (£150,000 each year); funded from Economic Development reserve £138,181, Corporate Plan priorities reserve £109,499, committed expenditure reserve £23,049, grants unapplied reserve £9,271, salary underspend transfer £20,000
